mcqs.question: In the grammar `Expr -> Expr PLUS Term | Term`, what role does `Term` play?
options: It is a non-terminal that can itself expand into further structure via its own production rules
It is a terminal token that must literally appear as the text "Term" in source code
It is a comment marker used only in grammar documentation
It is the grammar's designated start symbol
mcqs.explanation: Term is a non-terminal — a placeholder that expands via its own rules (shown for Term itself elsewhere in the topic), not literal source text. It isn't a terminal token, isn't documentation-only, and Expr, not Term, is the start symbol in this grammar.

mcqs.question: Why does translating `Expr -> Expr PLUS Term | Term` directly into a recursive-descent function cause infinite recursion?
options: Because PLUS is not a valid terminal symbol in recursive descent
Because recursive descent cannot handle any grammar rule with more than one alternative
Because parse_expr's first action would be calling parse_expr again, with no token consumed before that recursive call
Because Term's production rules conflict with Expr's
mcqs.explanation: Left recursion means the very first symbol on the right-hand side is the same non-terminal, so the corresponding function calls itself before consuming any input — the recursion never bottoms out. Multiple alternatives are fine in recursive descent generally, PLUS is a normal terminal, and there's no rule conflict between Term and Expr here.

mcqs.question: What does precedence climbing (Pratt parsing) let you avoid compared to writing one recursive-descent function per precedence level?
options: It avoids needing a lexer, parsing directly from raw characters
It avoids needing to define precedence for any operator, inferring it automatically
It avoids needing recursion entirely, using only iteration
It avoids writing a separate nested function for every precedence tier, using one loop driven by a numeric precedence table instead
mcqs.explanation: Precedence climbing collapses the whole ladder of per-level functions into one function with a precedence-driven loop, recursing only when a higher-precedence operator needs to bind first — genuinely less code for many precedence levels. It still needs a lexer and explicit precedence values, and it does still use recursion, just far less of it than one function per level.

mcqs.question: In shift-reduce parsing, what triggers a "reduce" action?
options: The parser runs out of input tokens entirely
The top of the stack matches the right-hand side of some grammar rule, so it's replaced by that rule's left-hand non-terminal
A syntax error is detected and the parser needs to recover
The lexer produces an invalid token
mcqs.explanation: Reduce happens exactly when the symbols on top of the stack form a complete match for some rule's right-hand side, at which point they collapse into that rule's non-terminal — this is the mechanism that builds structure bottom-up. Running out of tokens, error recovery, and lexer failures are separate concerns unrelated to what triggers an ordinary reduce.

mcqs.question: In the recursive-descent code, why does multiplication end up binding tighter than addition even though no explicit precedence numbers appear anywhere?
options: parse_expr calls parse_term, so any multiplication inside a term always finishes building before addition gets a chance to combine it with anything else
The tokenizer assigns implicit precedence values to each operator before parsing begins
Python evaluates * before + regardless of how the parser is structured
The BinOp constructor reorders operations based on operator type automatically
mcqs.explanation: Precedence falls directly out of the call structure — because parse_expr calls parse_term first, any multiplication is fully resolved into a single Term result before parse_expr's loop ever combines it with a PLUS or MINUS. Nothing in the tokenizer, Python's runtime, or BinOp is doing precedence work; it's entirely a property of which function calls which.

mcqs.question: `if (a) if (b) x(); else y();` is ambiguous under a naive if/else grammar. How do real languages resolve which `if` the `else` attaches to?
options: By convention: the else attaches to the nearest unmatched if, enforced by rewriting the grammar or a parser-generator precedence directive
The behavior is left undefined and varies by compiler
By always attaching else to the outermost if in the statement
By requiring explicit braces in every if statement, making the ambiguity impossible to write
mcqs.explanation: Every mainstream language deliberately resolves this the same way — nearest unmatched if — either via a grammar rewrite that makes it the only derivable parse or an explicit precedence rule in a generator's conflict table. Leaving it undefined would make basic control flow implementation-defined, attaching to the outermost if is not the convention used, and many languages don't require braces at all.
